name: Lisbon
tagline: Seven hills, trams and tiled streets
summary: Split Lisbon by hill: Alfama and the castle one day, Belém's monuments another, with a day trip to Sintra's palaces. Wear grippy shoes; the pavements are steep and slick.
seasonNote: July and August are hot and crowded; winter is mild but wet.
arrival: The metro's red line links the airport to the centre in about 30 minutes; taxis and ride-hailing are inexpensive.
gettingAround: Walk within each district and use the metro, trams and funiculars between hills. Tram 28 has long queues; ride it early or use it one way.
cashTip: Cards work almost everywhere; keep coins for small bakeries and kiosks.
foodTip: Try pastéis de nata warm, grilled sardines in season, bacalhau and a bifana sandwich.
buyTip: Tinned fish, cork goods and hand-painted tiles from shops that name the maker; never buy antique tiles from street sellers.

connections.note: Alfa Pendular and Intercidades trains from Santa Apolónia or Oriente; book ahead for the best fares.
Air time only; add airport transfers.
Limited direct flights; buses take about 6 to 7 hours.

items.name: Belém Tower
items.summary: A 16th-century river fortress that became the symbol of Portugal's age of exploration.
items.expect: Queues to go inside and narrow one-way stairs; the outside is the main event.
items.tip: See it from the riverside first and go in only if the queue is short.
items.why: Its carved stonework and setting on the Tagus make it the city's most recognisable landmark.
flow: Walk the riverside from the Monument to the Discoveries.
Circle the tower, then decide whether to climb.

items.name: Jerónimos Monastery
items.summary: A vast Manueline monastery with a two-storey cloister of carved limestone.
items.expect: Long ticket lines by mid-morning; the church is free and has its own queue.
items.tip: Buy a timed ticket online and arrive at opening.
items.why: The cloister is among the finest pieces of late Gothic stone carving in Europe.
flow: Visit the cloister with a timed ticket.
Step into the church to see Vasco da Gama's tomb.

items.name: São Jorge Castle
items.summary: Hilltop castle walls with the widest views over Lisbon's rooftops and river.
items.expect: A steep climb and little shade on the ramparts.
items.tip: Go late afternoon for softer light, then walk down through Alfama.
items.why: The ramparts give the best orientation to the city's hills in a single visit.
flow: Walk the ramparts and towers.
Descend through Alfama's lanes to a viewpoint.

items.name: Alfama and Miradouro de Santa Luzia
items.summary: Lisbon's oldest quarter: stairways, laundry lines, fado houses and tiled viewpoints.
items.expect: Steep cobbles and tuk-tuk traffic on the main lanes.
items.tip: Wander without a route and stop at Santa Luzia and Portas do Sol viewpoints.
items.why: It survived the 1755 earthquake, so its medieval street plan is intact.
flow: Start at Portas do Sol viewpoint.
Drift downhill towards the cathedral.

items.name: National Tile Museum
items.summary: Five centuries of Portuguese azulejo tiles in a former convent with a gilded church.
items.expect: Slightly out of the centre; allow for a bus or taxi.
items.tip: Don't miss the 23-metre tile panorama of Lisbon before the earthquake.
items.why: It explains the tilework you see on every street in the country.
flow: Follow the galleries in date order.
Finish in the convent church and the café courtyard.

items.name: Sintra and Pena Palace
items.summary: A day trip to a wooded hill town of palaces, topped by the yellow-and-red Pena Palace.
items.expect: Very busy in summer; shuttle buses and timed entry add waiting.
items.tip: Take an early train from Rossio and book Pena's timed ticket in advance.
items.why: Pena is Europe's most theatrical Romantic palace, set in a forested park.
flow: Train to Sintra, then bus 434 up to Pena.
Add Quinta da Regaleira or the Moorish Castle if time allows.

items.name: Pastéis de Belém
items.summary: The bakery that has made the original custard tarts since 1837.
items.expect: A takeaway queue that moves fast; the tiled rooms inside often have space.
items.tip: Skip the street queue and sit inside for table service.
items.why: The recipe is the original for Portugal's most famous pastry and is still made here by hand.
flow: Order tarts warm with cinnamon and sugar.
Eat in the tiled back rooms.

items.name: Time Out Market Lisboa
items.summary: A food hall of stalls from well-known Lisbon chefs and classic local names.
items.expect: Crowded communal tables at peak hours and prices above neighbourhood taverns.
items.tip: Come off-peak, grab seats first, then order from several stalls.
items.why: It lets a group sample many Portuguese dishes in one stop.
flow: Walk a full lap before ordering.
Share plates from two or three stalls.
items.best: Outside the busiest lunch or dinner hour.

items.name: Cervejaria Ramiro
items.summary: A loud, no-frills seafood hall famous for garlic clams, prawns and crab.
items.expect: A ticketed queue at the door and seafood priced by weight.
items.tip: Go at an off hour and finish, as locals do, with a steak sandwich.
items.why: It is the city's benchmark for simply cooked Atlantic shellfish.
flow: Take a ticket and wait for a table.
Order shellfish by weight, then a prego to finish.
items.book: Reserve if offered; small counters and popular lunch spots can have queues.

items.name: A Ginjinha
items.summary: A standing-room bar that has poured sour cherry liqueur since 1840.
items.expect: A counter and a pavement crowd; there are no seats.
items.tip: Ask for it 'com elas' if you want cherries in the glass.
items.why: A one-euro tradition that takes five minutes and sits in the heart of the old centre.
flow: Order a shot at the counter.
Drink it on the square outside.

name: Porto
tagline: Port cellars and a riverside of tiles
summary: Keep Porto compact: the Ribeira riverside and bridge, the tiled churches uptown, and the port lodges across the river in Gaia. Add a Douro Valley day for vineyards.
seasonNote: Atlantic rain is common from November to March; summer is warm rather than hot.
arrival: Metro line E runs from the airport to Trindade in about 30 minutes.
gettingAround: Walk, but expect hills; the metro, funicular and Gaia cable car save the steepest climbs.
cashTip: Cards are widely accepted; some small tascas prefer cash.
foodTip: Share a francesinha, try tripas or grilled fish in Matosinhos, and taste tawny against ruby port.
buyTip: Port bought at the lodges, tinned fish, and cork or filigree from named makers.

connections.note: From Campanhã station; book ahead for the best fares.
Air time only; add airport transfers.

items.name: Ribeira and Dom Luís I Bridge
items.summary: A double-deck iron bridge over the Douro with the old riverside quarter at its foot.
items.expect: Crowds on the quay and a shared upper deck with metro trains.
items.tip: Cross the top deck at sunset and come back along the lower one.
items.why: The view from the upper deck takes in the whole stacked old town.
flow: Walk the Ribeira quay.
Climb or ride up and cross the upper deck to Gaia.

items.name: Livraria Lello
items.summary: A 1906 bookshop with a carved, curving red staircase and stained-glass ceiling.
items.expect: Timed vouchers and a packed interior for most of the day.
items.tip: Book the first slot; the voucher comes off the price of a book.
items.why: It is one of the most beautiful bookshop interiors anywhere.
flow: Enter with a timed voucher.
Climb the staircase and browse the upper gallery.

items.name: São Bento Station
items.summary: A working station whose hall is lined with 20,000 blue-and-white tiles of Portuguese history.
items.expect: A short stop, busy with tour groups.
items.tip: Pair it with a regional train to the Douro or Guimarães.
items.why: The tile panels are the city's best free artwork.
flow: Read the panels around the main hall.
Step onto the platforms for the iron roof.

items.name: Clérigos Tower
items.summary: A baroque bell tower with 225 steps to a full-circle view of Porto.
items.expect: A narrow spiral stair with two-way traffic.
items.tip: Go early or at the last entry to avoid waiting on the stairs.
items.why: It is the highest viewpoint in the old centre.
flow: Visit the church and small museum.
Climb to the balcony.

items.name: Port lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia
items.summary: Cellar tours and tastings at the historic port houses across the river.
items.expect: Tours in set languages at set times; the best-known houses sell out.
items.tip: Book one in-depth tour rather than several quick tastings.
items.why: All port wine is aged here, and the lodges explain the styles before you taste them.
flow: Cross the bridge to Gaia.
Tour a lodge, then taste a tawny and a vintage side by side.

items.name: Douro Valley
items.summary: Terraced vineyards along the Douro, reached by scenic train, boat or tour.
items.expect: A long day; independent travel limits how many estates you can reach.
items.tip: Take the train to Pinhão for the views, or a small-group tour for estate visits.
items.why: It is one of the world's oldest demarcated wine regions and a World Heritage landscape.
flow: Travel upriver to Régua or Pinhão.
Visit an estate and take a short boat trip.
items.best: May to October; harvest in September

items.name: Café Santiago
items.summary: A plain café regarded as one of the best places for Porto's francesinha.
items.expect: Queues at meal times and a very heavy plate.
items.tip: Share one francesinha between two with fries.
items.why: The meat-stuffed, cheese-covered sandwich in beer sauce is the city's signature dish.
flow: Queue or arrive off-peak.
Order a francesinha with egg and a small beer.
items.best: Outside the busiest lunch or dinner hour.

items.name: Majestic Café
items.summary: A 1921 Belle Époque café of mirrors, leather banquettes and carved wood.
items.expect: High prices for coffee and cake; you pay for the room.
items.tip: Come for a mid-morning coffee rather than a full meal.
items.why: It is Porto's grandest historic café interior.
flow: Wait to be seated.
Order coffee and a pastry and take in the room.

items.name: Mercado do Bolhão
items.summary: The restored central market: produce, fish, cheese and snack counters under iron galleries.
items.expect: Busy late morning; most stalls close by early evening and on Sundays.
items.tip: Graze: oysters, cured meats, a glass of wine and a pastry from different stalls.
items.why: It is the best single place to see and taste northern Portuguese produce.
flow: Walk the ground-floor stalls.
Pick snacks and eat at the standing tables.

items.name: Casa Guedes
items.summary: A small tavern known for slow-roast pork sandwiches with mountain cheese.
items.expect: A short queue and few seats at the original bar.
items.tip: Ask for the sandes de pernil with Serra cheese.
items.why: It is the city's favourite cheap, quick lunch.
flow: Order at the counter.
Eat on the terrace with a glass of vinho verde.
order: Sandes de pernil com queijo da Serra

name: Madrid
summary: Build Madrid around its three art museums and long, late meals. Mornings for the Prado or palace, afternoons in Retiro, evenings moving between tapas bars.
seasonNote: July and August are very hot and many family restaurants close in August.
arrival: Metro line 8, the airport express bus and Cercanías trains all reach the centre in 30 to 40 minutes.
gettingAround: The centre is walkable and the metro covers the rest. Dinner starts after 9 pm.
cashTip: Cards are accepted nearly everywhere, including most bars.
foodTip: Have a bocadillo de calamares, tortilla, jamón ibérico and churros with thick chocolate.
buyTip: Espadrilles, saffron, good olive oil and vacuum-packed jamón (check customs rules for meat).
baseArea: Sol, Barrio de las Letras or Malasaña

connections.note: High-speed AVE, Iryo and Ouigo trains from Atocha; book ahead.
Air time only; add airport transfers.

items.name: Prado Museum
items.summary: Spain's national art museum: Velázquez, Goya, El Greco and Bosch.
items.expect: A huge collection; without a plan the visit becomes tiring.
items.tip: Book a timed ticket and pick 15 works; the last two hours are free but crowded.
items.why: Las Meninas, Goya's Black Paintings and The Garden of Earthly Delights are all here.
flow: Start with Velázquez on the first floor.
Finish with Goya's Black Paintings.

items.name: Royal Palace of Madrid
items.summary: The largest royal palace in western Europe, with state rooms, an armoury and a grand staircase.
items.expect: Security queues and occasional closures for state events.
items.tip: Check the closure calendar and book the first slot.
items.why: Its throne room and Tiepolo ceilings show Bourbon Spain at full scale.
flow: Tour the state apartments.
See the armoury, then the Sabatini Gardens.

items.name: Retiro Park
items.summary: The city's central park, with a boating lake, rose garden and the glass Crystal Palace.
items.expect: Lively at weekends, with buskers and families.
items.tip: Rent a rowing boat early, then walk to the Crystal Palace.
items.why: It is where Madrid relaxes, and a calm break between museums.
flow: Enter by the Puerta de Alcalá.
Walk from the lake to the Crystal Palace.

items.name: Reina Sofía Museum
items.wiki: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía
items.summary: Modern Spanish art, centred on Picasso's Guernica, with Dalí and Miró.
items.expect: A crowd around Guernica; no photos in that room.
items.tip: Go straight to the second floor for Guernica, then explore.
items.why: Guernica is the 20th century's defining anti-war painting.
flow: See Guernica and its preparatory sketches.
Continue through the Dalí and Miró rooms.

items.name: Plaza Mayor and Puerta del Sol
items.summary: The arcaded 17th-century main square and the busy crossroads beside it.
items.expect: Tourist-priced café terraces on the square itself.
items.tip: Look, then eat in the side streets or the nearby market.
items.why: It is the historic heart of Habsburg Madrid.
flow: Walk through the arches into the square.
Continue to Puerta del Sol and kilometre zero.

items.name: Toledo
items.summary: A hilltop former capital of churches, synagogues and mosques, half an hour away by fast train.
items.expect: Steep lanes and many day-trippers at midday.
items.tip: Book the train both ways; they sell out at weekends.
items.why: Three faiths left monuments side by side in one small walled city.
flow: Train from Atocha, then bus or escalators up.
Cathedral, Jewish quarter and the view from across the river.

items.name: Chocolatería San Ginés
items.summary: Churros and thick hot chocolate, served almost around the clock since 1894.
items.expect: A queue that moves quickly; several rooms.
items.tip: Come late at night or mid-afternoon for a shorter wait.
items.why: It is the city's classic churros stop.
flow: Pay first at the till.
Take a marble table and dip.

items.name: Sobrino de Botín
items.summary: Listed as the world's oldest restaurant (1725), roasting suckling pig in the original wood oven.
items.expect: A tourist favourite; the food is traditional and rich.
items.tip: Book well ahead and ask for the cellar dining room.
items.why: The oven has not gone out in three centuries and the roasts are still very good.
flow: Arrive for your booked time.
Order roast suckling pig or lamb to share.

items.name: Mercado de San Miguel
items.summary: An iron-and-glass market hall of tapas, seafood and vermouth counters.
items.expect: Crowded and pricier than neighbourhood bars.
items.tip: Treat it as a quick tasting stop, not dinner.
items.why: It gathers a wide range of Spanish bites under one handsome 1916 roof.
flow: Do a lap first.
Pick two or three bites and a vermouth.
items.best: Outside the busiest lunch or dinner hour.

items.name: Casa Lucio
items.summary: A classic tavern on Cava Baja famous for huevos rotos, broken eggs over fried potatoes.
items.expect: Old-school service and a dining room full of regulars.
items.tip: Reserve, or tapas-hop the rest of Cava Baja instead.
items.why: Its egg dish is copied all over Spain.
flow: Reserve a table.
Order huevos rotos to share, then a roast or stew.

name: Seville
tagline: Orange trees, flamenco and Moorish palaces
summary: See the Alcázar and cathedral early, rest through the hot afternoon, and come out again for tapas and flamenco. The old centre is flat and best on foot.
seasonNote: Summer regularly passes 40°C. Holy Week and the April Fair bring peak prices.
arrival: The airport bus reaches the centre in about 35 minutes; Santa Justa station has high-speed trains.
gettingAround: Walk; use the tram, bike share or taxis for longer hops.
cashTip: Cards are common; small bars may have a minimum spend.
foodTip: Order tapas a few at a time: salmorejo, spinach with chickpeas, fried fish and the pringá sandwich.
buyTip: Hand-painted ceramics from Triana, fans and olive oil.
baseArea: Santa Cruz, El Arenal or Alameda

connections.note: Air time only; the direct train takes about 5.5 hours.
Limited direct flights; buses take 6 to 7 hours.

items.name: Royal Alcázar of Seville
items.summary: A royal palace of Mudéjar courtyards, tilework and walled gardens, still in use.
items.expect: Timed tickets that sell out days ahead in spring.
items.tip: Book the first slot online and bring ID that matches the ticket.
items.why: It is the finest Mudéjar palace in Spain and rivals the Alhambra for detail.
flow: Go through the Patio de las Doncellas and Ambassadors' Hall.
Leave time for the gardens.

items.name: Seville Cathedral and Giralda
items.summary: The world's largest Gothic cathedral, with a former minaret you climb by ramp.
items.expect: Queues without a timed ticket; shoulders and knees covered.
items.tip: Book online; the Giralda's 35 ramps are easier than stairs.
items.why: It holds Columbus's tomb and gives the best view in the old city.
flow: See the main altarpiece and Columbus's tomb.
Climb the Giralda, then leave through the orange-tree courtyard.

items.name: Plaza de España
items.summary: A sweeping 1929 semicircle of brick, bridges and tiled alcoves for each Spanish province.
items.expect: Open and sunny, with little shade at midday.
items.tip: Visit early or near sunset and continue into María Luisa Park.
items.why: It is the city's most photogenic space, and free.
flow: Walk the curve of tiled province benches.
Cross the bridges, then stroll the park.

items.name: Barrio Santa Cruz
items.summary: The old Jewish quarter: whitewashed lanes, tiny squares and hidden patios.
items.expect: Easy to get lost, and busy with tour groups mid-morning.
items.tip: Wander in the evening when the day-trippers have gone.
items.why: Its narrow lanes were built for shade and are the most atmospheric walk in Seville.
flow: Start from the Alcázar walls.
Find Plaza de Doña Elvira and Callejón del Agua.

items.name: Metropol Parasol (Las Setas)
items.summary: A giant wooden canopy with a rooftop walkway over the old town.
items.expect: A short visit; the walkway is ticketed.
items.tip: Go at sunset and stay for the lights after dark.
items.why: It gives a modern rooftop view to contrast with the Giralda.
flow: Take the lift from the basement level.
Follow the looping walkway.

items.name: Triana
items.summary: The potters' and flamenco quarter across the river, with a market and ceramic workshops.
items.expect: A local feel; workshops close for the afternoon break.
items.tip: Cross Isabel II Bridge in the morning for the market, or at dusk for riverside bars.
items.why: It is the home of Seville's ceramics and much of its flamenco tradition.
flow: Cross the bridge to Triana market.
Walk Calle Betis along the river.

items.name: El Rinconcillo
items.summary: Seville's oldest bar (1670), where waiters chalk your bill on the wooden counter.
items.expect: Standing room at the bar; tables are in a separate dining room.
items.tip: Stand at the bar for the full experience.
items.why: Three and a half centuries on, it still serves classic tapas well.
flow: Find a spot at the bar.
Order two or three tapas and a sherry.
items.best: Early in the lunch or evening service

items.name: Bodega Santa Cruz (Las Columnas)
items.summary: A crowded, cheap tapas bar near the cathedral with orders shouted over the counter.
items.expect: Noise, elbows and no table service.
items.tip: Order at the bar and take plates to the street tables.
items.why: It is good value in the middle of the tourist zone.
flow: Push to the bar and order.
Eat standing or at a barrel outside.
items.best: Outside the busiest lunch or dinner hour.

items.name: Mercado de Triana
items.summary: A neighbourhood market by the bridge with produce stalls and small tapas bars.
items.expect: Liveliest late morning; quiet on Sunday.
items.tip: Have a late-morning tapa and sherry among the stalls.
items.why: A local-feeling food stop, built over the ruins of the Inquisition castle.
flow: Walk the produce aisles.
Sit at a market bar.

items.name: Eslava
items.summary: A popular tapas bar known for inventive, prize-winning small plates.
items.expect: A wait for the bar; it does not take bookings for tapas.
items.tip: Arrive right at opening.
items.why: It shows the modern side of Sevillian tapas at fair prices.
flow: Queue for opening.
Order the slow-cooked egg on mushroom cake and the honey rib.
items.book: Reserve if offered; small counters and popular lunch spots can have queues.

name: Amsterdam
summary: Book the Anne Frank House and Van Gogh Museum well ahead, then fill the gaps with canal walks and the Jordaan. Everything central is within a 30-minute walk or a short tram.
seasonNote: Tulip season runs mid-March to early May; summer is busiest and winter is dark and damp.
arrival: Trains from Schiphol reach Centraal in 15 to 20 minutes.
gettingAround: Walk or take trams; watch for bike lanes before stepping off a kerb.
cashTip: Many places are card-only; some do not take credit cards, so carry a debit card too.
foodTip: Try a fresh stroopwafel, herring from a stall, bitterballen with beer and Indonesian rijsttafel.
buyTip: Aged Gouda, stroopwafels and Delft-style ceramics from reputable shops.
baseArea: Jordaan, the canal ring or De Pijp

connections.note: Direct Eurostar high-speed trains; book ahead.
Direct trains several times a day.

items.name: Rijksmuseum
items.summary: The national museum, home to Rembrandt's Night Watch and Vermeer's Milkmaid.
items.expect: Timed entry and crowds in the Gallery of Honour.
items.tip: Book the first slot and go straight to the second floor.
items.why: It holds the greatest collection of Dutch Golden Age painting.
flow: Start in the Gallery of Honour.
Then the Delftware, ship models and library.

items.name: Van Gogh Museum
items.summary: The world's largest Van Gogh collection, arranged through his life.
items.expect: Tickets only online, often sold out a week or more ahead.
items.tip: Book as soon as dates are fixed; late afternoon slots are calmer.
items.why: Sunflowers, The Bedroom and Almond Blossom hang with his letters and sketches.
flow: Follow the floors in date order.
Finish with the last paintings from Auvers.

items.name: Anne Frank House
items.summary: The canal house and secret annex where Anne Frank hid and wrote her diary.
items.expect: Tickets released online about six weeks ahead, gone within hours; steep stairs.
items.tip: Set a reminder for the Tuesday ticket release.
items.why: It is one of the most moving historic sites in Europe.
flow: Walk through the warehouse and offices.
Pass the bookcase into the annex.

items.name: Canal Ring and Jordaan
items.summary: The 17th-century ring of canals, gabled houses and bridges, with the Jordaan's lanes beside it.
items.expect: Bikes everywhere; boats fill up on sunny days.
items.tip: Walk the Nine Streets, then take a small open-boat cruise near dusk.
items.why: The planned canal belt is a World Heritage site and the city's defining sight.
flow: Walk Prinsengracht and the Nine Streets.
Take a one-hour canal cruise.

items.name: Vondelpark
items.summary: The city's favourite park, with ponds, lawns and café terraces.
items.expect: Fast cyclists on the main path.
items.tip: Pair it with the museums next door.
items.why: An easy green pause that shows everyday Amsterdam.
flow: Enter from the Museumplein side.
Loop the ponds and stop at a terrace.

items.name: Zaanse Schans
items.summary: Working windmills and green wooden houses on a river, 20 minutes by train.
items.expect: Coach-tour crowds from late morning.
items.tip: Arrive before 10 am and pay to go inside one working mill.
items.why: It is the easiest place to see traditional Dutch windmills in action.
flow: Train to Zaandijk Zaanse Schans and walk over the bridge.
Visit a mill, the clog workshop and cheese farm.

items.name: Winkel 43
items.summary: A corner café famous for deep apple pie with whipped cream.
items.expect: Queues on Saturday and Monday market days.
items.tip: Take a slice on the terrace by Noordermarkt.
items.why: It is widely called the best apple pie in the city.
flow: Order at the bar if busy.
Have pie with cream and coffee.

items.name: Foodhallen
items.summary: An indoor food market in a former tram depot, with around 20 stalls.
items.expect: Loud and full on weekend evenings.
items.tip: Go for a late lunch and try the bitterballen stall.
items.why: It suits groups who all want something different.
flow: Find seats, then split up to order.
Share small plates.

items.name: Albert Cuyp Market
items.summary: The city's biggest street market, with stroopwafels made fresh, herring and poffertjes.
items.expect: Closed on Sunday; busiest at Saturday lunchtime.
items.tip: Get a warm stroopwafel from the stall that presses them to order.
items.why: The best place to snack through Dutch street food classics.
flow: Walk the full length.
Stop for a stroopwafel, herring and fries.

items.name: Café 't Smalle
items.summary: A 1786 'brown café' with a tiny canal-side terrace.
items.expect: Few seats; the terrace fills in good weather.
items.tip: Come mid-afternoon for a beer and bitterballen.
items.why: It is a classic example of Amsterdam's old wood-panelled pubs.
flow: Take a table inside or on the water.
Order a local beer or jenever with snacks.
